 Trey Kaufman-Renn and Kansas are into our top five after an impressive win over Kentucky. Michael Reaves / Getty Images 
 By CJ Moore Nov. 12, 2026 Updated 8:17 am EST Share article 41 Early in the season is always the most difficult time to rank teams. Sample sizes are small. It’s hard not to overreact to results. Teams make big jumps up and down the board.
 Most voters have a bias toward their preseason polls, and while some bias of that is healthy, it’s best to look at teams with fresh eyes early.
 Advertisement
 Duke, for instance, moved into the No. 1 spot after blowing out Tennessee and winning at Kansas in the preseason. With more data points now, that was probably an overreaction. For one, I’m much lower than consensus on Tennessee . Two, Kansas was playing without Trey Kaufman-Renn, who has totally changed the Jayhawks. And three, there’s reason to be skeptical of the Blue Devils based on who they lost and what skill they lost. (More on that later.)
 A reminder that my weekly Top 25 does not feature all 25 teams. This week’s featured teams: Florida, Kansas, Michigan State, Texas Tech, Illinois, St. John’s and Vanderbilt.
 Dropped out from preseason ranking : Iowa, Iowa State, Purdue 
 Keeping an eye on: West Virginia, Iowa State, Nebraska, Tennessee, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oklahoma State, USC, Florida State 
 1. Florida
 Florida is shooting 39.2 percent so far from 3-point range, which is notable because it shot just 31.2 percent last year. The Gators are thriving from the corners, making 17-of-27 from that area of the floor, according to Synergy.
 The Gators are 5-for-5 when defenses are helping on post-ups, which creates easy reads for the guards and long closeouts for the defense:
 Florida’s bigs do an excellent job running to the rim and posting up early in transition, often leading to easy shots at the basket because of "Gortats" (screening off their man), but those post-ups will also generate these open shots. This is another example of how hard Florida’s bigs play every possession and why the Gators are so difficult to guard. Even when they aren’t scoring at the basket, they’re helping to win games.
 5. Kansas
 KU’s offensive identity has completely changed in the last few weeks. Everything is now built around Purdue transfer Trey Kaufman-Renn as the hub. Charting KU’s half-court possessions against Kentucky showed that TKR got a touch on 27 of the 33 possessions he was on the floor, with Kansas scoring 31 points on the 27 possessions he got a touch.
 Advertisement
 Kaufman-Renn shot, got fouled or set up the end of the possession through a pass, ball screen or dribble-handoff on 24 of those possessions.
 Possessions Points 
 Ball screen 2 0 
 DHO 6 5 
 Pass 10 12 
 P&R 3 5 
 Post-up 1 0 
 Offensive rebound 2 4 
 Total 24 26 
 Those aren’t bad results in the half court, but they’re likely to get even better as his new teammates get used to playing with him. Remember, he showed up to campus on Oct. 19. His feel and vision make the game easier for everyone else, and Bill Self will continue to dream up new ways to take advantage of his playmaking abilities.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Tyran Stokes chose Kansas over Kentucky. The Jayhawks’ romp over the Wildcats showed why
 Stokes picked the system and coach to get the best out of him, as he showed on Tuesday night when Kansas ran Kentucky off the floor.
 6. Michigan State
 Tom Izzo looks to have an elite defense and a breakout defensive star in Jordan Scott. Michigan State had 16 deflections against Duke and Scott had seven of those. The Spartans also had nine blocks by my count, and Scott had six.
 Duke struggled to screen Scott because he plays so tight against ballhandlers and is confident in his ability to stay in front of anyone. Good luck trying to get a shot over him. This is what it looks like when he puts it all together:
 Jordan Scott's becoming a defensive star The Spartans played with the kind of effort, physicality and awareness that leads to great defense, and no one was better than Scott. He dominated the game and only scored 5 points.
 9. Texas Tech
 Texas Tech averaged more points per game hitting the roller (9.5) than any team in the country last season, per Synergy. This year, its rollers have scored only 12 points in three games. That will likely change once JT Toppin is healthy.
 What hasn't changed is that offensive coordinator Jeff Linder is spamming high ball screens with his lead guard. Last year Christian Anderson led college basketball in using pick-and-rolls 20.9 times per game, according to Synergy. This season, Hofstra transfer Cruz Davis leads all high-major players with 22 per game.
 The approach is different. Christian Anderson was more of a processor, using a hang dribble to decide what he was going to do next:
 Christian Anderson's approach For Davis, the Red Raiders are setting ball screens higher up the floor to utilize his speed. It’s difficult to catch up if his man gets clipped by the screen:
 Cruz Davis' approach Davis cannot match Anderson in terms of vision and feel, but his speed will be an issue, especially once defenses also have to worry about Toppin.
 Advertisement
 10. Duke
 Through three games, Duke is shooting 30.1 percent from 3 and made just 7-of-29 against Michigan State.
 We probably should have seen this coming. Duke lost its best four 3-point shooters off last year’s team — Isaiah Evans, Cameron Boozer, Nikolas Khamenia and Darren Harris. The returners shot 33.5 percent from deep last year. Duke did add John Blackwell, who made 96 3s at a 38.9 percent clip last season at Wisconsin, and first-year Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje is a capable shooter who will probably shoot it better than he has so far. But the lack of floor spacers was evident against the Spartans, who were not worried about Cayden Boozer, allowing Jeremy Fears Jr. to play free safety and muck up action when Boozer was his assignment.
 The Blue Devils have the potential to be elite defensively, but they must figure out what to do about its shooting and the absence of a true go-to guy. The Michigan State loss was one bad night against an elite defense, and on nights when Blackwell and Boumtje Boumtje are hitting, Duke could look like a title contender. But not retaining Khamenia or Harris could be something Jon Scheyer ends up regretting.
 11. Illinois
 This is probably too low for Illinois. It's not really fair to judge the Illini until David Mirkovic, expected to be Brad Underwood’s best player, returns from a foot injury.
 One reason not to worry about the Illini: Last season’s team shot 78 percent from the free-throw line, 17th-best in college basketball. The Illini are shooting 56.9 percent in three games this year, including an 8-for-19 stinker in their 84-78 loss at Texas Tech. Stefan Vaaks, an 83.9 percent free-throw shooter at Providence, went 2-for-6 in that game and is 4-for-12 overall. That’s not likely to continue.
 14. St. John’s
 Rick Pitino signed a 23-year-old starting point guard out of the EuroLeague in Quinn Ellis. What's the value of handing the keys to a guy with that kind of experience? Ellis has 27 assists and just two turnovers in three games.
 16. Vanderbilt
 Vanderbilt's biggest weakness last season was rebounding, so Mark Byington tried to address that by signing three transfers who were 6-foot-9 or taller, in addition to 6-10 freshman Jackson Sheffield. Byington has gone from playing a rotation with one player at 6-9 or taller to five.
 So far, Vandy is boarding:

 2025-26 68.5 232 31.2 158 
 2026-27 78.3 21 41.2 28 
 What’s scary is what happened to Memphis in a 105-81 loss at Vanderbilt. The Commodores made 21-of-31 2s, 15-of-32 3s and got back 12 of their 29 misses. That’s how you hang 105 on what looks to be a quality team.
